reads.label: Inflation
reads.why: Inflation sets how much room the Fed has, and the Fed sets the discount rate applied to every future cash flow on earth. It is first in the chain because everything else is downstream of it.
reads.means: Inflation is the constraint on everything else: it sets how much room the Fed has, and the Fed sets the discount rate on every asset. While inflation is above target, weak growth data is not rescued by the Fed quickly, so bonds and equities can fall together - the correlation that made 2022 unusual.
reads.watch: CPI and core PCE prints; the dot plot at SEP meetings.

reads.label: Growth & labour

evidence.label: Atlanta Fed GDPNow
evidence.note: current quarter, rebuilt as data lands

reads.why: Growth drives earnings, and the labour half of it is the other side of the Fed's mandate. When labour data deteriorates, the Fed's reaction function flips from fighting inflation to defending employment - which is the single most important regime change there is.
reads.means: Growth decides earnings, and jointly with inflation it decides which way the Fed leans. Solid growth supports earnings but removes the urgency to ease, so the market has to pay for earnings rather than for rate cuts.
reads.watch: Weekly claims every Thursday; payrolls on the first Friday.

reads.label: Monetary policy
reads.state: mildly restrictive, market pricing hikes (real policy rate +0.54pp vs ~0.5pp neutral; 2-year +0.88pp vs funds)

evidence.label: Fed funds (effective)
evidence.note: the anchor for every discount rate

evidence.label: 2-year Treasury yield
evidence.note: the market's forecast of the path

evidence.label: SOFR (overnight repo)
evidence.note: funding plumbing; a spike forces Fed action

reads.why: The policy rate is the price of money and the base of every valuation. What matters is not its level but its level relative to inflation, and what the market already expects it to do next.
reads.means: The real policy rate - funds minus core inflation - is what 'restrictive' actually means; the nominal level on its own says nothing. The 2-year yield minus the funds rate is the market's own forecast of the path, and it moves months before the Fed does. With little easing priced in, a weak data run has room to rally bonds without needing the Fed to say anything.
reads.watch: Eight scheduled FOMC decisions a year; the SEP meetings move the curve most.

reads.label: Rates & the curve

evidence.label: 2s10s curve
evidence.note: which end is moving is the signal

reads.why: Long yields are where policy expectations, inflation expectations and the government's borrowing needs are priced together. Equities discount off them, so the composition of a rate move decides whether it is survivable.
reads.means: The 10-year is the discount rate for everything, and WHICH END of the curve moves tells you why. Bull steepening (front end falling) is the market pricing cuts and has historically been the best environment for bonds and for small caps. Bear steepening (long end rising) is term premium or fiscal risk and is the hardest kind of rate rise for equities to absorb, because the discount rate goes up without any growth to pay for it.
reads.watch: Auctions and the quarterly refunding announcement; every inflation print.

reads.label: Credit & conditions
reads.state: wide open, arguably complacent (8th percentile of the last 5 years)

evidence.label: Investment-grade OAS
evidence.note: widening here means it is not idiosyncratic

evidence.label: Banks tightening C&I standards
evidence.note: how rate rises reach small business

reads.why: Credit is the transmission belt. A slowdown with open credit markets is a slowdown; a slowdown with closed ones is a recession. It also happens to lead equities.
reads.means: Credit decides whether a slowdown becomes a default cycle. While spreads are tight, weak companies refinance and nothing breaks; when they widen, refinancing stops and the slowdown feeds itself. Credit has led equities into every serious drawdown, and high-yield spreads widening while investment grade follows is the specific pattern that distinguishes a market event from a single-sector problem.
reads.watch: Daily spreads; bank earnings for loan-loss provisions; the quarterly loan officer survey.

reads.label: Liquidity

evidence.label: Treasury General Account
evidence.note: government cash: fills and drains on a schedule

reads.why: The quantity of reserves in the system determines how much leverage the market can carry. Liquidity drains are slow, scheduled and knowable in advance - and then abrupt when something breaks.
reads.means: Liquidity is the quantity side of policy, and it works with a lag and then all at once: reserves fall slowly for months and then a funding market seizes, as repo did in September 2019. It is also the most predictable thing on this page, because Treasury's cash schedule and the Fed's runoff caps are both published in advance.
reads.watch: The Fed's H.4.1 every Thursday; tax dates; any change to runoff caps.

reads.label: Risk appetite
reads.state: risk-on (volatility low, index above its 200-day average)
reads.why: What the market currently believes, as revealed by what it is paying for. Most useful when it contradicts the fundamentals above, because that gap is where positioning risk lives.
reads.means: Risk appetite is the output of everything above, which makes it a poor input: it tells you what is already priced, not what happens next. Its use is as a cross-check - when leadership disagrees with the index (defensives leading a rising market, small caps lagging a rally), the index is usually the part that is wrong. Low volatility is also not safety: it is when leverage accumulates, which is what makes the next shock larger.
reads.watch: Nothing scheduled - this one reacts to the others.

regime.summary: inflation sticky above target; growth expanding; monetary policy mildly restrictive, market pricing hikes; rates positive curve, flattening; credit wide open, arguably complacent; liquidity flat; risk appetite risk-on.
regime.tension: The reads are broadly consistent with each other, which means the market is priced roughly where the data says it should be - and the next scheduled release matters more than usual.
regime.disclaimer: These are readings of public data and descriptions of how each one has historically transmitted to asset prices. They are not advice about what to buy, sell or hold.

calendar.title: Initial jobless claims
calendar.detail: The only weekly read on the labour market, barely revised, and a genuine leading indicator - firms file before a monthly survey can see it. Use the 4-week average; the weekly number is seasonal noise. (Date inferred: Department of Labor publishes every Thursday.)

calendar.title: Conference Board consumer confidence
calendar.detail: More labour-market-weighted than the Michigan survey, so the 'jobs hard to get' component is the part with signal - it tracks the unemployment rate with a short lead. (Date inferred: Conference Board publishes on the last Tuesday of the month.)

calendar.title: Personal income & outlays (core PCE)
calendar.detail: The Fed's actual target measure, and the one its own forecasts are written in. It arrives two weeks after CPI, so the surprise is usually small - but when PCE and CPI disagree, PCE is the one policy follows. (Date inferred: BEA publishes near the end of the month for the prior month.)

calendar.title: ISM manufacturing PMI
calendar.detail: A survey, so it is fast rather than accurate - and because it is a diffusion index, 50 is the line between expansion and contraction. The prices-paid component is an early inflation read the Fed watches. (Date inferred: ISM publishes on the first business day of the month.)

calendar.title: Initial jobless claims
calendar.detail: The only weekly read on the labour market, barely revised, and a genuine leading indicator - firms file before a monthly survey can see it. Use the 4-week average; the weekly number is seasonal noise. (Date inferred: Department of Labor publishes every Thursday.)

calendar.title: Employment Situation (payrolls)
calendar.detail: Payrolls, unemployment rate, participation and average hourly earnings in one release, which is why it can move rates twice in opposite directions inside a minute. The revisions to the prior two months frequently matter more than the headline; the 3-month average is the honest read. (Date inferred: BLS publishes on the first Friday of the month.)

calendar.title: ISM services PMI
calendar.detail: Services are the larger and stickier half of the economy, and the half where this cycle's inflation has lived. A services PMI holding above 50 while manufacturing sits below it has been the normal state, not a warning. (Date inferred: ISM publishes on the third business day of the month.)

calendar.title: FOMC minutes
calendar.detail: Released three weeks after the decision. Where the range of views inside the committee becomes visible - a hawkish minority that did not make the statement shows up here.

calendar.title: 10-year Treasury auction
calendar.detail: A weak auction - a high yield versus the pre-auction market, poor bid-to-cover, dealers left holding the paper - is how supply pressure becomes a same-day equity event. (Date inferred: Treasury auctions the 10-year mid-month, usually the Wednesday of the week containing the 9th.)

calendar.title: Initial jobless claims
calendar.detail: The only weekly read on the labour market, barely revised, and a genuine leading indicator - firms file before a monthly survey can see it. Use the 4-week average; the weekly number is seasonal noise. (Date inferred: Department of Labor publishes every Thursday.)

calendar.title: 30-year Treasury auction
calendar.detail: The long bond has the thinnest genuine demand of any Treasury, so it is where fiscal scepticism shows up first. (Date inferred: Treasury auctions the 30-year the day after the 10-year.)

calendar.title: JOLTS job openings
calendar.detail: Vacancies per unemployed worker is the measure behind the Fed's bet that it could cool wages without mass layoffs. Two months stale, so it settles arguments rather than starting them. (Date inferred: BLS publishes about six weeks after the reference month.)

calendar.title: U. Michigan sentiment (preliminary)
calendar.detail: A weak forecaster of spending but a closely watched one, because its inflation-expectations components are cited in Fed speeches. Read those sub-indices, not the headline. (Date inferred: University of Michigan publishes the preliminary reading on the second Friday.)

calendar.title: CPI (consumer prices)
calendar.detail: The most heavily traded number of the month. Watch the month-over-month core rate, not the annual headline: 0.2% keeps a cutting cycle alive and 0.4% ends the argument. Shelter is a third of the index and lags reality by about a year, so a surprise usually comes from services elsewhere. (Date inferred: BLS publishes the prior month between roughly the 10th and 15th.)

calendar.title: Earnings season opens (big banks)
calendar.detail: The large banks report first and their loan-loss provisions, net interest margins and consumer-credit commentary are the earliest bottom-up read on credit for the whole quarter. (Date inferred: The largest banks report in the second week of January, April, July and October.)

calendar.title: Beige Book
calendar.detail: Anecdotal reports from the twelve Reserve Banks, two weeks before the decision. Rarely moves a market, but it is the last thing the Fed publishes before the communications blackout, and its language often turns up verbatim in the statement.

calendar.title: PPI (producer prices)
calendar.detail: Costs upstream of the consumer, and the source of several PCE components CPI does not measure - so a hot PPI moves core PCE forecasts the same morning. Also the cleanest monthly read on corporate margins. (Date inferred: BLS publishes a day or two after CPI.)

calendar.title: Retail sales
calendar.detail: Two thirds of the economy is consumption and this is the monthly read on it. Nominal, so compare it to inflation, and look at the control group that feeds GDP rather than the headline. (Date inferred: Census publishes mid-month for the prior month.)

calendar.title: Housing starts & building permits
calendar.detail: The most rate-sensitive part of the economy, and it has led most postwar recessions. Permits lead starts, and single-family leads multi-family. (Date inferred: Census publishes around the 17th.)

calendar.detail: Large open interest rolling off can move the index mechanically and usually releases volatility that dealer hedging had been suppressing. It is flow, not information - do not read it as a signal about anything. (Date inferred: Third Friday of every month.)

brief.disclaimer: These are readings of public data and descriptions of how each one has historically transmitted to asset prices. They are not advice about what to buy, sell or hold.

metrics.label: Core PCE inflation
metrics.why: The Fed targets 2% on the PCE deflator, and it is core PCE - food and energy stripped out - that the FOMC's own projections forecast. Every other inflation number is ultimately a guess at this one.
metrics.up_means: Later and fewer rate cuts. Pushes the whole yield curve up and compresses what investors will pay for distant earnings.
metrics.down_means: Room for the Fed to cut without losing credibility, which is the single most reliable tailwind for long-duration assets.
metrics.watch: 2% is the target. Above ~2.8% y/y the committee has historically stopped easing; below ~2.3% cuts get justified on inflation alone.

metrics.label: Core PCE, 3-month annualised
metrics.why: A year-over-year rate is an average of twelve months, so it keeps reporting last spring for most of a year. The 3-month annualised rate is the same data asked 'what is inflation doing right now', and it is what turns a Fed pause into a cut two meetings early.
metrics.up_means: Momentum is re-accelerating even if the annual rate is still falling. This is the read that has repeatedly caught the market leaning the wrong way.
metrics.down_means: Disinflation is live, not a base effect.
metrics.watch: Sustained prints under 2.5% annualised are what the committee has called 'further progress'; over 3.5% is a policy problem.

metrics.label: Core CPI inflation
metrics.why: Two weeks earlier than PCE and far more heavily traded, so it is the print that actually moves a given day. Shelter is about a third of it and lags reality by roughly a year, which is why CPI and PCE can disagree for quarters at a time.
metrics.up_means: Immediate repricing of the Fed path; the front end of the curve moves first and hardest.
metrics.down_means: Relief rally in both bonds and equities, usually within the same minute the number crosses.
metrics.watch: The monthly change matters more than the level: 0.2% keeps a cutting cycle alive, 0.4% ends the conversation.

metrics.label: Headline CPI inflation
metrics.why: What households actually experience, and therefore what drives surveys, wage demands and politics. The Fed looks past it; voters and bond vigilantes do not.
metrics.up_means: Political pressure and higher inflation expectations even when core is behaving.
metrics.down_means: Real incomes rise, which supports consumption without needing the Fed to do anything.
metrics.watch: Gaps versus core are almost always energy. Check oil before concluding anything about underlying inflation.

metrics.label: PPI final demand
metrics.why: Costs upstream of the consumer, and the source of several PCE components that CPI does not measure. A useful early read on margins: when PPI runs below CPI, companies are keeping the difference.
metrics.up_means: Margin pressure, and pipeline inflation that reaches PCE later.
metrics.down_means: Margin relief - often good for equities even when demand is soft.
metrics.watch: The healthcare and portfolio-management components feed PCE directly; a hot PPI can move PCE forecasts the same morning.

metrics.label: 10-year breakeven inflation
metrics.why: What the bond market itself prices for average inflation over ten years - nominal yield minus the TIPS yield. Unlike a survey it is money at risk, and unlike a print it updates every second.
metrics.up_means: The market doubts the Fed will hold the line, or expects a supply shock. Nominal bonds lose, real assets win.
metrics.down_means: Either credibility, or a demand scare. Check oil and credit spreads to tell which - both falling together means demand.
metrics.watch: 2-2.5% is the Fed's comfort zone. Above 2.75% the Fed has historically talked hawkish regardless of the spot data.

metrics.label: 5y5y forward breakeven
metrics.why: Expected inflation for the five years starting five years from now: far enough out that today's oil price and today's cycle wash out. This is the cleanest available measure of whether the Fed still owns the anchor.
metrics.up_means: Anchor slipping - the most serious inflation signal there is, and the one that justifies policy staying tight into weakness.
metrics.down_means: Long-run credibility intact, whatever the spot prints say.
metrics.watch: A move outside roughly 2-2.5% is the thing to care about; wiggles inside it are noise.

metrics.label: Average hourly earnings
metrics.why: Wages are the input to services inflation, which is the sticky half. Pay growth running far above productivity growth has to end up in either prices or margins.
metrics.up_means: Services inflation stays sticky; the Fed's job is not finished.
metrics.down_means: Disinflation becomes self-sustaining rather than a goods-price story.
metrics.watch: Roughly 3.5% y/y is consistent with 2% inflation given trend productivity. Persistently above 4% is not.

metrics.label: Fed funds (effective)
metrics.why: The price of overnight money, and the anchor every other discount rate is built on. It is set by eight scheduled decisions a year, which is why an FOMC date is the most predictable market-moving event on the calendar.
metrics.up_means: Tighter policy: higher hurdle rate for every investment, and a direct hit to the multiple on long-duration cash flows.
metrics.down_means: Easier policy, but read WHY it is easing - cuts into a recession and cuts into a soft landing are different trades.
metrics.watch: Compare to core inflation: funds minus core PCE is the real policy rate, and that difference, not the level, is what 'restrictive' means.

metrics.label: Fed funds target (upper)
metrics.why: The committee's stated ceiling. Worth tracking alongside the effective rate because a persistent gap between them is a money-market plumbing signal, not a policy one.
metrics.up_means: A hike has landed.
metrics.down_means: A cut has landed.
metrics.watch: The effective rate drifting to the top of the band is an early sign that reserves are getting scarce.

metrics.label: SOFR (overnight repo)
metrics.why: What secured overnight funding actually costs. It is the plumbing gauge: a spike means collateral or reserves are short, which has twice forced the Fed to act between meetings.
metrics.up_means: Funding stress. Small moves are quarter-end noise; a sustained spread over the funds target is not.
metrics.down_means: Ample reserves.
metrics.watch: SOFR printing above the top of the funds target band, especially away from quarter-end.

metrics.label: Fed balance sheet
metrics.why: The quantity side of policy. Shrinking it drains reserves from the banking system, which tightens conditions without touching the policy rate - and the market usually notices the effect before the cause.
metrics.up_means: Reserves added. Historically supportive of risk assets, whatever the stated reason.
metrics.down_means: Quantitative tightening is draining liquidity; the effect is slow and then sudden, as 2019's repo squeeze showed.
metrics.watch: The weekly change matters more than the level. Watch it together with reserve balances and the Treasury cash account.

metrics.label: Bank reserve balances
metrics.why: The actual buffer in the system, and the variable the Fed says it is steering when it decides how far quantitative tightening can go. Scarce reserves are how a liquidity drain becomes a market event.
metrics.up_means: More cushion; funding markets calm.
metrics.down_means: The system is running closer to the edge. This is the series to watch when people argue about when QT has to stop.
metrics.watch: Reserves falling while the Treasury cash account rises is a drain with a known end date - and a known reversal.

metrics.label: Overnight reverse repo
metrics.why: Cash parked at the Fed overnight by money funds. For two years it was the shock absorber that let the Treasury issue heavily without draining bank reserves. Near zero, that cushion is gone and new issuance hits reserves directly.
metrics.up_means: Idle cash rebuilding - usually a sign bills are cheap relative to the Fed's floor.
metrics.down_means: The buffer is being spent. Once empty, liquidity drains show up in reserves and then in risk assets.
metrics.watch: How close it is to zero, not the change.

metrics.label: Treasury General Account
metrics.why: The government's own checking account. When it fills - tax dates, a rebuild after a debt-ceiling fight - cash leaves the private system; when it is spent down, liquidity returns. It is the most predictable liquidity swing there is, because the schedule is published.
metrics.up_means: Liquidity leaving the private system.
metrics.down_means: Liquidity returning.
metrics.watch: Mid-April and mid-quarter tax dates, and any post-debt-ceiling rebuild.

metrics.label: M2 money supply
metrics.why: A slow, much-abused aggregate - but its 2020-21 surge and 2022-23 contraction did bracket the inflation wave, and it remains a useful sanity check on liquidity narratives built from weekly noise.
metrics.up_means: Nominal spending power growing.
metrics.down_means: Historically rare and associated with disinflation, sometimes with recession.
metrics.watch: Direction over quarters. Anyone trading this weekly is fooling themselves.

metrics.label: 2-year Treasury yield
metrics.why: The market's forecast of average policy over two years. It is the cleanest read on what traders think the Fed will do, and it moves before the Fed does - every cutting cycle in living memory was priced here first.
metrics.up_means: The market is pulling cuts out or adding hikes. Front-end pain, and pressure on anything financed short.
metrics.down_means: Cuts being priced in. Good for bonds; for equities it depends entirely on whether growth data is falling too.
metrics.watch: 2-year minus fed funds is the implied path: materially below the funds rate means the market expects cuts.

metrics.label: 10-year Treasury yield
metrics.why: The global discount rate. Mortgages, corporate hurdle rates and equity valuations are all quoted off it. Since 2022 the correlation has flipped: a fast rise in the 10-year is now an equity event, not a hedge.
metrics.up_means: Multiples compress, long-duration growth equities and housing hurt first. Whether it is a growth or an inflation move decides if it is survivable.
metrics.down_means: Supportive for valuations - unless it is falling because growth is, in which case earnings are the bigger problem.
metrics.watch: Speed over level. Roughly 50bp in a month has historically been enough to break an equity rally regardless of where it started.

metrics.label: 30-year Treasury yield
metrics.why: Where fiscal credibility shows up. The long end is priced by buyers who care about deficits and issuance rather than the next meeting, so a long end rising while the front end falls is a term-premium story - the bond market charging more to fund the government.
metrics.up_means: Term premium rebuilding. Historically the hardest kind of rate rise for equities to absorb.
metrics.down_means: Confidence in long-run inflation and issuance.
metrics.watch: 30-year rising on a day the 2-year falls. That specific pattern is the fiscal-stress tell.

metrics.label: 10-year real yield (TIPS)
metrics.why: The nominal yield with expected inflation taken out - the actual cost of long-term money. It is the correct discount rate for equity cash flows, and it separates 'rates rose because of growth' from 'rates rose because of inflation fear'.
metrics.up_means: Genuine tightening. This is the variable that has done most of the damage to long-duration equities and to gold.
metrics.down_means: Real easing, even if headline yields are unchanged.
metrics.watch: Above roughly 2% real, historically, is where valuation-sensitive assets start to struggle.

metrics.label: 2s10s curve
metrics.why: Ten-year yield minus two-year. Inversion has preceded every US recession since the 1960s, but the more useful signal is the re-steepening: recessions have tended to arrive as the curve un-inverts, not while it is inverted.
metrics.up_means: Steepening. Bull steepening (front end falling) means cuts are coming; bear steepening (long end rising) means term premium or inflation risk.
metrics.down_means: Flattening or inverting - policy tight relative to growth. Squeezes bank margins and anything borrowing short to lend long.
metrics.watch: Which end is doing the moving. The level alone tells you much less than the composition.

metrics.label: 3m10y curve
metrics.why: The version of the curve the New York Fed's own recession model uses, and the one least contaminated by expectations about the very front end.
metrics.up_means: Normalising.
metrics.down_means: Deeper inversion.
metrics.watch: Sign changes rather than wiggles.

metrics.label: 30-year mortgage rate
metrics.why: How monetary policy reaches most households. It also gates the existing-home market through lock-in: owners holding 3% loans do not list at 7%, so supply, transactions and everything downstream of them freeze.
metrics.up_means: Affordability and transaction volumes fall; builders, brokers, lenders and home-improvement demand all feel it.
metrics.down_means: The most direct channel for a rate cut to reach the real economy, with roughly a two-quarter lag.
metrics.watch: 6% is roughly where refinancing waves and normal turnover restart.

metrics.label: High-yield OAS
metrics.why: The extra yield demanded to lend to junk-rated companies. This is the market's honest opinion about default risk, and it is the single best early-warning gauge on this list: credit has led equities into every serious drawdown, and it does not do false positives quietly.
metrics.up_means: Risk being repriced. A move through 500bp has historically coincided with equity drawdowns rather than preceded them by much - which is exactly why the direction matters daily.
metrics.down_means: Credit is open: companies can refinance, which removes the mechanism by which a slowdown becomes a default cycle.
metrics.watch: Roughly 300bp is complacent, 500bp is stress, 800bp+ is a crisis. The rate of change matters more than the level.

metrics.label: Investment-grade OAS
metrics.why: The same question asked of the companies that actually fund the economy. When investment-grade spreads widen, the problem has stopped being idiosyncratic.
metrics.up_means: Stress reaching quality borrowers - a genuine escalation.
metrics.down_means: Funding conditions benign.
metrics.watch: Widening at the same time as high yield is a market event; high yield alone is usually an energy or single-name story.

metrics.label: Chicago Fed financial conditions
metrics.why: One number summarising 105 measures of risk, credit and leverage. Useful precisely because it is hard to talk yourself out of: it aggregates the plumbing you would otherwise cherry-pick from.
metrics.up_means: Conditions tightening versus history - a headwind that operates with a lag of quarters.
metrics.down_means: Conditions loosening. Note that loosening conditions are what make a central bank keep policy tighter for longer.
metrics.watch: Zero is average since 1971. Positive is tighter than average.

metrics.label: St. Louis Fed financial stress
metrics.why: A second, differently-built stress index. Two independent gauges agreeing is worth far more than either one moving alone.
metrics.up_means: Stress building.
metrics.down_means: Calm.
metrics.watch: Zero is the historical average; sustained positive readings are rare.

metrics.label: Banks tightening C&I standards
metrics.why: The Fed asks loan officers directly whether they are making it harder to borrow. Quarterly and slow, but it is the mechanism by which rate rises actually reach small business - and it leads business investment by two to three quarters.
metrics.up_means: Credit being rationed. Small and mid-cap earnings feel this long before large caps do.
metrics.down_means: Credit opening up - a necessary condition for a capex recovery.
metrics.watch: Net percentages above ~20% tightening have accompanied every recent recession.

metrics.label: Nonfarm payroll change
metrics.why: The most-traded number in macro, and the one the Fed's employment mandate is written against. It is also heavily revised, which is why the three-month average is the honest read and the headline is the tradeable one.
metrics.up_means: A hot print pushes cuts further out - good for earnings, bad for multiples. Which effect wins depends on where inflation is.
metrics.down_means: Cuts pulled forward. Below roughly zero, the market stops treating weakness as good news and starts pricing recession.
metrics.watch: Breakeven job growth - enough to hold unemployment flat - is roughly 100k and has been falling with immigration. Compare to the 3-month average, not to last month.

metrics.label: Unemployment rate
metrics.why: Half of the Fed's mandate, and the input to the only recession rule with a decent record: the Sahm rule fires when the 3-month average rises half a point above its low of the prior year. Labour markets do not deteriorate gently.
metrics.up_means: The Fed's reaction function flips from inflation to jobs. Cuts get faster and bigger, and earnings estimates start falling.
metrics.down_means: Tight labour market, wage pressure, less urgency to ease.
metrics.watch: The rise off the 12-month low, not the level. Half a point is the line.

metrics.label: Initial jobless claims (4wk avg)
metrics.why: The highest-frequency read on the labour market: weekly, barely revised, and a genuine leading indicator because firms file before they show up in a monthly survey. This is how you find out a turn is happening without waiting three weeks.
metrics.up_means: Layoffs broadening. Sustained rises have preceded every unemployment-rate turn.
metrics.down_means: Firms are holding onto workers, whatever the survey data says.
metrics.watch: Use the 4-week average - the weekly number is seasonal noise. A move above roughly 260k has historically marked genuine deterioration.

metrics.label: Continuing claims
metrics.why: Initial claims say whether people are losing jobs; continuing claims say whether they are finding new ones. In a low-firing, low-hiring labour market this is the half that is actually deteriorating.
metrics.up_means: Re-employment is getting harder - the slow way a labour market cracks.
metrics.down_means: Displaced workers are being absorbed.
metrics.watch: Rising continuing claims with flat initial claims is the classic late-cycle signature.

metrics.label: Job openings (JOLTS)
metrics.why: Vacancies per unemployed worker is the measure the Fed leaned on to argue it could cool wages without mass layoffs - the 'Beveridge curve' bet. Watching openings fall without unemployment rising is watching that bet pay off.
metrics.up_means: Labour demand still strong; wage pressure persists.
metrics.down_means: Cooling without firing, if unemployment holds. Once openings are back to normal, further cooling has to come from layoffs.
metrics.watch: Openings per unemployed worker near 1.0 is a balanced market.

metrics.label: Quits rate
metrics.why: Workers quit when they are confident of something better. It leads wage growth by a couple of quarters and is a cleaner confidence read than any survey, because it costs something to be wrong.
metrics.up_means: Job-switching wage premium returning; services inflation stickier.
metrics.down_means: Workers sitting tight - falling wage pressure, and a household sector that will spend more cautiously.
metrics.watch: Roughly 2.3% is the pre-pandemic norm; below it is a cautious labour market.

metrics.label: Labour force participation
metrics.why: Determines whether a falling unemployment rate is good news. People leaving the workforce lowers the rate without anyone getting a job, and it changes how much employment growth the economy needs.
metrics.up_means: More supply of labour - disinflationary, and allows faster growth without wage pressure.
metrics.down_means: A tighter effective labour market than the headline suggests.
metrics.watch: Prime-age (25-54) participation is the version not distorted by demographics.

metrics.label: U-6 underemployment
metrics.why: Includes part-time-for-economic-reasons and discouraged workers. When U-6 rises faster than U-3, the labour market is weakening in hours before it weakens in headcount - which is how this cycle has tended to do it.
metrics.up_means: Slack building beneath the headline.
metrics.down_means: Genuine full employment.
metrics.watch: The U-6 minus U-3 gap, not either level.

metrics.label: Real GDP growth
metrics.why: The scoreboard, published so late that it mostly confirms what markets already traded. Its value is in the composition: growth driven by consumption and investment is durable, growth driven by inventories and net exports is not.
metrics.up_means: Earnings support, less need for easing.
metrics.down_means: Earnings estimates come down; the Fed's employment mandate starts to bind.
metrics.watch: Final domestic demand strips out the noisy components and is the number worth reading.

metrics.label: Atlanta Fed GDPNow
metrics.why: A running estimate of the current quarter, rebuilt every time a monthly input lands. It is the antidote to GDP's publication lag: mechanical, transparent and updated before the fact rather than after.
metrics.up_means: Incoming data is running hotter than consensus.
metrics.down_means: The current quarter is tracking below what equity analysts have in their models.
metrics.watch: Early-quarter readings are noisy by construction. It gets useful once several months of inputs are in.

metrics.label: Retail sales
metrics.why: Two thirds of the US economy is consumption, and this is the monthly read on it. Nominal, so compare to inflation: sales growing 3% with 3% inflation means real volumes are flat.
metrics.up_means: The consumer is absorbing higher rates. Supports earnings and keeps the Fed cautious.
metrics.down_means: Demand destruction reaching the consumer - and the consumer is what has held this cycle up.
metrics.watch: The 'control group' excluding autos, gas and building materials is what feeds GDP.

metrics.label: Real consumer spending
metrics.why: Retail sales with inflation removed and services included - the honest version of whether consumption is growing.
metrics.up_means: Real demand growing; earnings revisions tend to follow.
metrics.down_means: Volumes falling even if revenue lines still grow.
metrics.watch: Compare to real disposable income: spending growing faster means the savings rate is falling, which cannot continue indefinitely.

metrics.label: Industrial production
metrics.why: Manufacturing is a sixth of the economy but a much larger share of its volatility, and it turns earlier. It is also the part most exposed to tariffs, the dollar and global demand.
metrics.up_means: Goods cycle recovering - usually good for cyclicals, energy and industrial metals.
metrics.down_means: Goods recession, which has repeatedly happened without a broader one.
metrics.watch: Manufacturing weakness alongside strong services has been this cycle's normal state, not a warning.

metrics.label: U. Michigan sentiment
metrics.why: Consumers' own view. A weak forecaster of spending - people spend when they have income, not when they feel good - but its inflation expectations component is watched closely by the Fed, and it is increasingly a read on politics.
metrics.up_means: Confidence improving, marginally supportive of discretionary spending.
metrics.down_means: Historically a poor recession signal on its own. Do not trade it alone.
metrics.watch: The 1-year and 5-10 year inflation expectation sub-indices matter more than the headline.

metrics.label: S&P 500
metrics.why: The benchmark, and also a policy input: the Fed watches financial conditions, and equity prices are a large part of them. Its level relative to its own 200-day average is the crudest useful trend filter in existence.
metrics.up_means: Wealth effect, easier financial conditions - which paradoxically allows the Fed to stay tighter for longer.
metrics.down_means: Tightening conditions. A drawdown that reaches credit spreads is the kind that changes Fed behaviour.
metrics.watch: Distance from the 200-day average, and whether breadth confirms - an index carried by five names is a different market.

metrics.label: VIX
metrics.why: The price of one month of S&P options - the market's own estimate of how much it is about to move. It is mean-reverting and usually low, which is exactly why a sustained rise matters: it means hedging has become expensive because someone needs it.
metrics.up_means: Demand for protection. Spikes are usually the end of a move rather than the start, but a grind higher from a low base is a regime change.
metrics.down_means: Complacency. Persistent lows have historically been when leverage builds up, which is what makes the next shock larger.
metrics.watch: Below 15 is calm, above 25 is stress, above 35 is a liquidity event. The shape of the futures curve says more than the level.

metrics.label: Broad dollar index
metrics.why: The dollar is the global funding currency, so its price is a global financial condition. A strong dollar tightens conditions everywhere, squeezes emerging markets, cuts the foreign earnings of US multinationals and pushes commodity prices down.
metrics.up_means: Global tightening. Bad for emerging markets, commodities and roughly 40% of S&P revenue.
metrics.down_means: A global easing impulse, and usually the start of international equities outperforming.
metrics.watch: Why it is moving: rate differentials, growth differentials or a safe-haven bid all point to different trades.

metrics.label: EUR/USD
metrics.why: The largest single weight in the dollar index, and mostly a story about the gap between Fed and ECB policy.
metrics.up_means: Dollar weakening against the euro.
metrics.down_means: Dollar strength or European weakness.
metrics.watch: The 2-year yield spread between Germany and the US explains most of it.

metrics.label: USD/JPY
metrics.why: The world's carry trade. Cheap yen funding finances leveraged positions everywhere, so a sharp yen rally has repeatedly forced global de-leveraging - August 2024 being the clearest recent case.
metrics.up_means: Yen weakening: carry trade profitable, leverage building.
metrics.down_means: Carry unwinding. Fast yen strength is a global risk event regardless of what Japan intended.
metrics.watch: The speed of a move, and Bank of Japan or Ministry of Finance comments about intervention.

metrics.label: WTI crude
metrics.why: The fastest route from geopolitics to headline inflation to consumer spending. An oil spike is a tax on consumption and an inflation problem at the same time, which is the one combination monetary policy handles worst.
metrics.up_means: Headline inflation up, real incomes down, central banks cornered. Energy equities are the hedge.
metrics.down_means: Disinflationary and supportive of consumption - unless it is falling because global demand is.
metrics.watch: Whether it is moving on supply (geopolitics, OPEC) or demand (China, global growth). The same price move means opposite things.

metrics.label: Brent crude
metrics.why: The international benchmark, and the one that prices most of the world's physical barrels. A widening Brent-WTI spread is usually a US logistics or export story.
metrics.up_means: Global supply tightness.
metrics.down_means: Global demand softness.
metrics.watch: The spread to WTI.

metrics.label: Housing starts
metrics.why: Residential construction is small in GDP but enormous in cyclicality, and it is the most rate-sensitive part of the economy. It has led most postwar recessions.
metrics.up_means: Rate relief reaching the real economy; good for materials, labour demand and the mid-cycle story.
metrics.down_means: The rate channel is biting. Watch permits to see whether it continues.
metrics.watch: Permits lead starts, and single-family leads multi-family.

metrics.label: Building permits
metrics.why: The intentions version of housing starts, and therefore the leading half of a leading indicator.
metrics.up_means: Builders committing capital - a genuine confidence signal because it is expensive to be wrong.
metrics.down_means: Pipeline shrinking.
metrics.watch: Single-family permits specifically.

metrics.label: Case-Shiller home prices
metrics.why: Housing is most households' entire balance sheet, so prices drive the wealth effect far more broadly than equities do. The index is also a three-month average reported with a two-month lag - the slowest number on this list.
metrics.up_means: Wealth effect supports consumption; shelter inflation stays sticky with a long lag.
metrics.down_means: Negative wealth effect and eventually falling shelter CPI.
metrics.watch: Remember the lag. This tells you about last quarter.

metrics.label: Existing home sales
metrics.why: Transaction volume, which is what actually generates economic activity - brokers, movers, renovations, appliances. Rate lock-in has held this near multi-decade lows regardless of demand.
metrics.up_means: The freeze thawing; a broad activity boost.
metrics.down_means: Lock-in intact.
metrics.watch: This is about mortgage rates, not about prices.

metrics.label: Monthly federal deficit
metrics.why: Deficits have to be funded, and funding means Treasury issuance. Issuance sets the supply of duration the market must absorb, which is a direct input to the long end of the curve and to the term premium.
metrics.up_means: A larger deficit means more issuance and, at the margin, a higher long-end yield.
metrics.down_means: Less supply pressure.
metrics.watch: Monthly numbers are wildly seasonal - use the 12-month rolling total. The quarterly refunding announcement is where issuance plans actually become news.

metrics.label: Federal debt outstanding
metrics.why: The stock behind the flow. It matters through interest expense: as low-coupon debt rolls into today's yields, debt service crowds out everything else and becomes a fiscal-political constraint.
metrics.up_means: More supply to absorb, more interest expense.
metrics.down_means: Rare.
metrics.watch: Interest expense as a share of revenue is the number that eventually forces a decision.
